24.text: Of all these varieties, No. 1 is the most common; No. 3 is scarce,

25.text: especially on the tundra; No. 4 is very good fodder, but grows only in cer-

26.text: tain places; No. 5 is poorer fodder; Nos. 6 and 7 are good fodder, but they

27.text: grow only on burnt places, and are scarce.

28.text: With the first green sprouts that shoot up through the snow, the reindeer

29.text: cease to care for the moss, and scatter over considerable distances in search

30.text: of new kinds of food. In summer they feed on sprouts growing on the tundra,

31.text: chiefly on various species of reed-grass; also on young leaves of low willow-

32.text: bushes, shore-grass, and the like, with the exception, however, of common

33.text: grass, — “horse-fodder” (koˊnên-vaˊᵋg̣lɪñɪn) as the Chukchee call it. Even late

34.text: in the fall, reindeer require some reed-grass and withered leaves mixed with

35.text: moss, and without it they will not fatten. On the other hand, toward the

36.text: end of summer they require moss mixed with the grass, and without it they

37.text: will not thrive. This season is the most critical one for the herdsman, since

38.text: a herd that does not gather fat enough in late summer will not be able to

39.text: keep in condition through the whole winter, even in the best pastures, and

40.text: in the springtime will be in danger of losing all fawns on account of the

41.text: exhaustion of the dams. In the fall the reindeer has a great relish for mushrooms,

42.text: and seeks for them so obstinately as to neglect its ordinary fodder, and lose

43.text: fat. It also consumes bird-dung with relish, quantities of which are heaped

44.text: around the moulting-places of ducks. The Yukaghir on the Middle Omolon,
